_: Authored half of the final-cut read. The scene rows come from the platform's scene analysis when it returns; everything else is read from the project's own record — favourites, the post-deadline jobs, the uploads, the Predictor. Regenerate the page with design/build-final-cut.py.
intro: The board closed at 22:53 UTC on deadline day with 27 cards and a 5:43 plan. The film was not cut from it verbatim, and the project keeps a record of exactly how it wasn't: 31 favourites, fifteen generations made after the board closed, three uploads of the finished film, and Predictor scores on the takes that could be scored. This chapter reads that record against the two scene-clip artefacts the cut was made from — shot-board.html and the Canvas Boards page — and turns the differences into rules. The scene-by-scene read of the delivered file is added below the moment the platform's analyser returns it; the sections after it do not depend on it.

All three queued behind the platform's analyser and had not been picked up when this page was built. The read below is from the record, not from the picture; the diff rows say which.

feel.t: The editor's eye beat the board six times and the score never once
feel.p: Six favourites sit on takes the board had as alternates, and where both takes were scored the favourite was one point lower every time — 48 to 49, 51 to 52, 58 to 59 — which is noise. Where the board had a number the editor had a look, and the look won: S20 kept the first-read take after the rescoring had moved the pick. The board is a proposal; the timeline is the decision.

feel.t: The chase was fixed by regenerating, not by choosing
feel.p: S11, S7 and S10 were all regenerated after the board closed — S11 on deadline night, the other two the next day. The instinct every time was 'make it again on the right sheet', not 'take the other one'. It worked on S11 and cost nothing in score; it was not taken on S7; it is undecided on S10.

feel.t: The opening stayed on the older courtyard
feel.p: The four favourited S1 takes are the 30s v4.0 pair on the retired courtyard element and the Sep 8 Seedance pair. The board's one argument for f84a308f — element continuity with the S23 bookend — did not survive contact with the crane in the older takes. At a wide the two courtyards are one place.

feel.t: Order, durations and the three additions
feel.p: Whether the brothers' first five seconds play before the vortex, whether the tails were trimmed rather than the heads, and whether NEW-1, NEW-2 and NEW-4 are in the delivered cut are questions only the picture answers. The analyser has all three files; this card is replaced by its scene rows.

grade.p: Gold on black, then blue-grey with no warmth, then golden hour into crimson. The takes the cut favours are already graded inside the generation — the chroma S22, the dark-ground Movement II — so the grade's job in the NLE is a lift, not a look: match black level and highlight roll-off across neighbours and leave the colour alone.

S1 is on the old courtyard element and S23 on the new. Match them by the plasma — hue, black level, the haze density — not by the architecture, which nobody compares four minutes apart. A gold-and-black frame at the top and an identical gold-and-black frame at the end reads as one place.

The S11 regeneration is 1080p; its neighbours S10 and S12 are 1344×576. Do not sharpen the neighbours to meet it — soften the regeneration to meet them, a touch of halation on the highlights, and the join disappears. Sharpening 720p footage is how a cinematographer on the jury knows.

grade.t: Grade the takes, not the timeline
grade.p: Selection was the grade on this film — the chroma take over the flat take, ten points. On the next film, generate the chroma lane for every shot that carries the ending, pick from it, and give the NLE nothing to do but level-match.
One favourited take carries the model's own voice saying 'Thank you' in its last second. Solo every audio-on take's tail before the sound pass; a phantom line survives a grade and ruins a screening.

work_note: Fifteen jobs between the board closing and the Sep 16 upload. Four on deadline night, ten the following evening, one splice at 23:02. The board argued against one of them, wrote the prompts for six of them, and never saw any of them — every one is a decision the timeline made after the last artefact was built. ♥ marks the ones the cut favourited.
fav_note: Favourites are the cut's own record of what it used, and the only one the platform keeps. Read down the third column: where the board's pick is not favourited and an alternate is, the timeline overruled the board. Where nothing is favourited, the editor had one obvious take and did not mark it — nine shots, all of them in the middle of Movement II.

lessons.t: The board's pick lost six times, and never to the score
lessons.w: Six favourited takes were the board's alternates (S1, S12, S16, S18, S20, S22). Where both were scored the favourite was one point behind — noise. The editor took the first-read take every time; S11's two favourites are a regeneration, not a swap, because there was nothing to swap to.
lessons.r: Show the alternates at the pick's size, and write the pick as a proposal. A board that argues for one take is a board the editor stops reading; a board that lays four takes side by side is one they cut from.

lessons.t: Element continuity is invisible at a wide
lessons.w: The board picked the only S1 on the current courtyard element so the bookend would match. The cut favourited the 30s takes on the retired element, because the crane was better and the courtyard is the same picture at 21:9.
lessons.r: Rank continuity arguments by whether a viewer can see them at the shot's size. At a wide, motion and light outrank the element id; at a close-up, the element id is everything.

lessons.t: The fix was to regenerate, not to choose
lessons.w: S11 had one take, on the wrong sheet and too short. At 23:04 on deadline night it was regenerated four times on the battle sheet at 15s; two were favourited; the score did not move.
lessons.r: Keep a 'regenerate this clip on the right sheet' prompt ready for every shot with a face in it, before the deadline, and budget ten minutes for it. Picking around an identity break does not work when there is nothing to pick from.

lessons.t: A transition the board called redundant was made the next day
lessons.w: The board said NEW-3 was covered by the S6 take's match cut. On Sep 15 it was generated twice anyway, from the S4 take as a video reference, and favourited.
lessons.r: Never call a transition redundant on the board. Show both versions and let the timeline decide; a transition costs one generation and its absence costs a seam.

lessons.t: Phantom speech in a silent shot
lessons.w: One of the two favourited S11 regenerations carries the model's own audio saying 'Thank you' at 14–15s — a flank run with no dialogue in it.
lessons.r: Solo the last two seconds of every audio-on take before it goes in the timeline. Generated ambience can carry a voice, and it is inaudible in a browser tile.

lessons.t: The film was still being made two days after the deadline
lessons.w: The board closed at 22:53 on Sep 14. Six new takes, six regenerations and a splice followed on Sep 15; the MOV went into the project root on Sep 16; the low and HQ exports on Sep 18.
lessons.r: Write down which file was submitted and which file is in the project, by id and date, the day you submit. A project with three versions of the film and one submission needs a line saying which is which.

lessons.w: Nine shots — all in the middle of Movement II — have no favourite at all; the editor marked takes only where there was a choice to make.
lessons.r: Favourite the pick of every shot as you lay it, including the obvious ones. The record is only a record if it is complete, and it is the only one the platform keeps.

lessons.t: Two macro takes filed under the wrong shot for two weeks
lessons.w: The Sep 15 tear-to-ocean macros were attributed to the end card because both prompts begin 'Macro, locked'. The end-card plate was never generated at all.
lessons.r: Attribute by the whole prompt, not its first line, and check attribution against the favourites: a favourited take on a shot with no pick is a mis-filing until proved otherwise.

verdict: What the cut says about the board. The scene-clip artefacts were right about the spine — every Movement III pick but three held, the dialogue shots held, the chroma ending held — and wrong about their own authority. The editor treated the board as a proposal, overruled it on look six times, regenerated three shots rather than pick around them, and made the one transition it had argued against. None of that is a failure of the board; it is what a board is for. The failure is that the board did not know it was overruled: nothing wrote the timeline's decisions back. That is what the ninth stage on the Anchorframe desk now does — upload the master, read the favourites against the picks, run the scenes, and write every delta back as a lesson, a reminder, and an example. The next film starts from these rows, not from a clean board.
